title: Singapore’s core inflation eases to 1.5% in October
html:
Year-on-year overall inflation fell to 1.9% in October from the previous month’s 2.2%.

ST PHOTO: LIM YAOHUI

AI generated

SINGAPORE – Singapore’s overall inflation fell in October on lower price increases for services, electricity and gas, as well as private transport, even as prices for retail and other goods edged up.

Year-on-year core inflation slowed to 1.5% compared with September’s 2%, according to data released by the Singapore Department of Statistics on Nov 23.

On a month-on-month basis, October’s core prices remained unchanged. Core inflation excludes private transport and accommodation to better reflect household expenses.

Year-on-year overall inflation fell to 1.9% in October from 2.2% the previous month, driven by lower inflation in services, electricity and gas, and private transport. On a month-on-month basis, it fell 0.3%.

Private transport inflation slowed to 6.7% from September’s 7.1% due to a more gradual increase in car prices. Accommodation inflation held steady at 0.9% in October as housing rents rose at a similar pace as in September.

Services inflation dropped to 1.1% from September’s 1.7%, due to smaller increases in airfares, health insurance and healthcare services.

Inflation for retail and other goods, however, picked up to 1.6% from 1.2% the previous month, as furniture prices rose and household appliance prices fell at a slower pace.

Food inflation eased slightly to 2.3% from September’s 2.4%, as non-cooked food prices rose at a slower pace.

Electricity and gas inflation saw the sharpest drop, falling to 1% from September’s 8.7% as electricity costs rose more gradually in October.

The decline in year-on-year electricity inflation was largely due to a lower regulated electricity tariff in October than in September.

Standard Chartered economists wrote in a note dated Nov 23 that their guidance for core inflation has shifted from remaining “slightly elevated in the immediate quarters” to picking up in the first quarter of 2027, while their expectation of more discernible easing from mid-2027 remains unchanged.

Edward Lee, Stanchart’s chief economist and head of foreign exchange for ASEAN and South Asia, and Jonathan Koh, Stanchart’s senior economist and foreign exchange analyst for ASEAN, had four reasons for the change.

The first was that the fourth-quarter electricity-tariff reduction pushed core inflation lower than expected, which provided a “lower starting point for the projected pick-up”.

The second was to account for the adjusting of oil price movements in recent months, when oil prices surged in October before easing in November.

“The fourth quarter’s year-to-date Brent price average is US$102.80 per barrel of crude oil; if it stays at US$90 till mid-December, the October to mid-December Brent price average will be US$97.50. July to mid-September average was US$88.80,” Lee and Koh wrote.

They also took into account the 7% public transport hike that will take effect on Dec 26 – higher than the 5% hike of Dec 27, 2025.

Lastly, Lee and Koh wrote that El Nino – a weather phenomenon that typically brings hotter, drier conditions to South-east Asia and disrupts crop yields – could drive up food prices in the coming months.

The economists maintained their view of the Monetary Authority of Singapore keeping the status quo for policy settings at the January 2027 meeting, with the risk skewed towards further tightening.

However, they note that the risk of tightening is “less than before”, as the latest US restrictions on advanced chips and remote-compute access add uncertainty to the growth outlook, and could delay or disrupt regional data-centre investment and related equipment orders.

“There is also a risk that recent concerns over investment returns lead to lower capital expenditure, project delays or weaker orders,” they added.
summary: Services inflation slowed while retail and other goods’ inflation picked up.
